question: Since the Commission issued Regulation (EU) No 461/2010 aiming to curtail monopolistic practices in the automotive industry, the EU’s non-original spare parts market has grown significantly. Vehicle use costs and insurance payouts linked to repairs have fallen as a result, but questions remain about the impact of this market growth on road safety. 1.

Does the Commission think that the current information system on the quality of spare parts is reliable, and does it intend to precisely regulate the definitions specifying the quality of spare parts in comparison to original parts, or to create a list of spare parts whose parameters are particularly important to improving road safety, or to require manufacturers to certify spare parts so as to guarantee that they are genuinely comparable to original parts?

In the Commission’s view, does the failure to implement Annex VI to Regulation (EU) 2018/858 of the European Parliament and of the Council (‘List of parts or equipment that may pose a serious risk to the correct functioning of systems that are essential for the safety of the vehicle or its environmental performance...’) not constitute carte blanche to place parts on the market that may negatively impact road safety?

In the Commission’s opinion, are insurance companies that invoke Commission Regulation (EU) No 461/2010 misleading affected customers, and can it be said that the quality breakdown differentiating groups of parts of a similar quality no longer applies?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (19.11.2024) EU law1 requires non-original replacement parts with a critical bearing on safety and environment (e.g. tyres, brake pads and discs, light bulbs, catalytic converters) to meet the same requirements as original parts2.

Parts or equipment that may pose a serious risk to the correct functioning of systems essential for the vehicle safety or environmental performance must be authorised. Member States may maintain their national provisions until the Commission establishes, based on an evaluation, the list referred to in Article 55(4) of Regulation (EU) 2018/8583.

The Commission has the possibility to take safeguard measures to withdraw the authorisations granted to parts that may pose a serious risk. This issue was discussed at the Technical Committee for Motor Vehicles in 2020 where Member States expressed a strong preference to maintain the regulation of spare parts at national level.

This does not prevent the Commission from reassessing the situation in the future and making a proposal, if needed. Regulation (EU) No 461/20104 specifies the conditions under which motor vehicle spare parts distribution and repair and maintenance service agreements are exempted from the application of Article 101(1) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU5.

The associated Supplementary Guidelines (2010/C 138/05)6 provide detailed guidance on the interpretation of the Regulation. These documents do not mandate the use of particular parts for particular purposes, nor do they establish that any particular part is safe or of matching quality with those of original components.
1 In accordance with Article 50 of Regulation (EU) 2018/858 of the European Parliament and of the Council,

vehicle components and separate technical units, including those intended for the aftermarket, may only be made available on the market or entered into service if they comply with the requirements of the relevant regulatory acts listed in Annex II to the Regulation and are marked in accordance with Article 38.

2 For example, the General Safety Regulation (EU) 2019/2144 sets out requirements for the approval of replacement brake lining assemblies, drum brake linings and discs and drums. 3 OJ L 151, 14.6.2018, p. 1. 4 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:02010R0461-20230507 5 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:52014XC0830(01) 6 https://eur-lex.europa.
